title: Device flow emulator and adaptive NCCL overlap tuner for staged prefill-decode
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Goal: build a lightweight device-flow emulator that can reproduce cross-device token handoffs and NCCL traffic patterns seen in staged prefill-decode runs, and an adaptive overlap tuner that uses emulator + live telemetry to recommend and apply NCCL concurrency windows, microbatch sizing, and handoff pacing to reduce tail latency and improve throughput efficiency. Motivation: existing heuristics for overlap and handoff assume homogeneous links and steady compute; real clusters show link skew, PCIe/NVLink asymmetry, and noisy co-tenants leading to variable overlap effectiveness. The emulator enables safe offline tuning and regression testing; the tuner applies closed-loop adjustments during rollout to avoid regressions.
acceptance_criteria: Emulator: able to reproduce token-handoff traces (timestamps, bytes, kernel events) from production trace files with >=85% similarity on handoff timing and NCCL byte-waveform shape.
Tuner: automated policy that reduces 95th percentile prefill-decode latency by at least 10% on synthetic heterogeneous-link scenarios compared to current static heuristics.
Controls: rollout can be toggled per-customer/route and has an automatic rollback if latency or error rate regresses beyond configured thresholds.
Safety: all changes to NCCL window/concurrency applied via orchestrator and logged; no changes to model weights or kernel code.
Docs: short-run guide and observability dashboard panels for tuner decisions and emulator-mode comparisons are published in Console docs.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (emulator): ingest existing prefill-decode traces and implement a simulator that replays compute events, token handoffs, and NCCL byte transfers with configurable link bandwidth/latency/skew.

Phase 2 (tuner prototype): offline sweep runner that runs emulator with candidate {microbatch, window_size, concurrency_stride} combos and scores using cost function (tail latency + token-per-second efficiency).
Phase 3 (live integration): expose tuner as a runtime controller that observes token wave telemetry and applies soft changes via orchestrator (graceful window ramp, per-stage microbatch hints).
Phase 4 (observability): add dashboard panels: tuner decisions, predicted vs observed overlap, rollback triggers, and per-route latency delta.

PRs: initial emulator code in repo runtime/emulator (draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4127), tuner controller prototype in runtime/control (draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4132).
test_plan: Unit tests: deterministic emulator scenarios, injection of link anomalies, and validation of replay timestamps.
Integration: run emulator-based sweeps across a matrix of synthetic topologies: homogeneous 4xNVLink, mixed NVLink+PCIe, constrained interconnect with 30% effective bandwidth.
Canary: enable tuner for 5% of production routes with synthetic traffic shaping to evaluate real-world behavior for 48 hours before expanding to 25%.
Regression: run existing kernel-selection and batching regression suite to ensure no throughput loss on common workloads.
Performance baseline: collect end-to-end metrics (p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/s, NCCL throughput) and compare against static heuristics.
rollout_plan: 1. Internal canary: runtime cluster with isolated test tenants; validate rollback triggers and logs.
2. Gradual external canary: 5% -> 25% -> 100% per-route rollout with daily check-ins and automatic rollback if latency or error rate exceeds configurable thresholds.
3. Safe defaults: if tuner detects pathological link conditions, fall back to static conservative window sizes (current production heuristic).
4. Documentation: release notes for runtime-1.21 describing tuner knobs and observability panels.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: tuner misconfigures NCCl concurrency and increases tail latency unexpectedly. Mitigation: always apply changes as soft ramps with canary scope and immediate rollback triggers on delta > configured SLA.

Risk: emulator does not accurately model complex kernel-level overlaps leading to false positive tuning. Mitigation: use emulator only as a candidate generator; live telemetry must corroborate predicted gains before full rollout.
Risk: additional CPU/agent overhead for live tuner controller. Mitigation: lightweight controller implemented in Rust with bounded CPU budget and sampling of traces at 1% by default.
Risk: interaction with autoscaling/dedicated policies. Mitigation: add guardrails so tuner defers when autoscaler is executing or when Dedicated capacity churn > threshold.
